<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 9228, the Health Data Access, Transparency, and Affordability (Health DATA) Act of 2026, amends the Employee Retirement Income Security Act\1\ (ERISA) to increase access to data by fiduciaries of employer-sponsored health benefit plans. Although this legislation seeks to address the shared, bipartisan goal of improving health care transparency, it lacks needed safeguards that would ensure data is used appropriately and that workers and their families are protected from discrimination and retaliation based on their health information and medical records. Committee Democrats are therefore unable to support this legislation in its current form.
\1\Pub. L. No. 93-406 (1974).
The Majority's decision to advance H.R. 9228 in a partisan manner is a regrettable departure from past collaborations between Committee Democrats and Republicans on similar issues. During the 118th Congress, the Committee on Education and Workforce (Committee) worked in a bipartisan manner to develop similar legislation, also entitled the Health Data Access, Transparency, and Affordability (DATA) Act (H.R. 4527), introduced by Reps. Lori Chavez-DeRemer (R-OR), Kathy Manning (D-NC), and Mark Takano (D-CA). The bill was reported favorably to the House of Representatives by the Committee on July 12, 2023,\2\ but was not ultimately enacted prior to the conclusion of the 118th Congress. Rather than continuing this collaborative process during the 119th Congress, the Majority instead chose to develop H.R. 9228 on a partisan basis without even conferring with any Committee Democrats, including one of the original bill's co-authors, Rep. Takano. As a result of this unusual and unnecessarily partisan process, the legislation appropriated the name, but not the substance, of the bill from the 118th Congress, and it contains serious flaws that jeopardize the privacy of workers and their families.
\2\H. Rept. 118-260 (2023).
CONGRESS SHOULD FOCUS ON RISING HEALTH CARE COSTS, INCLUDING WASTEFUL
SERVICE PROVIDER FEES AND CONFLICTS OF INTERESTS
High health care costs represent an urgent issue for consumers across America, who increasingly face unaffordable health insurance premiums and out-of-pocket expenses. In 2024, total national health expenditures in the United States reached $5.3 trillion or 18.0 percent of gross domestic product.\3\ Individuals' per capita health care spending has risen to $14,775, approximately double the average amount spent per capita in peer countries.\4\ These expenditures are heavily driven by high prescription drug prices and the rates charged by hospitals, physicians, and other health care practitioners.\5\ Additionally, this growing health care spending is also directly correlated with rising administrative costs associated with service providers, particularly for individuals with private health coverage.\6\

\6\See Linda J. Blumberg et al., Untangling the Complex Web: Summary of a New Expert Perspective, Georgetown Ctr. on Health Ins. Reforms (Nov. 19, 2025), https://chir.georgetown.edu/untangling-the-complex-web-summary-of-a-new-expert-perspective/.
Employers who sponsor health plans often rely on a range of outside vendors who assist in administering and managing their plans. While many such service providers play a valuable role in delivering benefits, they can also be described as middlemen who create ``a complex web of common ownership, contracting arrangements, and financial deals which create an array of conflicts of interests and hidden flows of money.''\7\ These business models can have an inflationary effect on health care spending, ultimately at the expense of consumers who must shoulder rising premiums and cost-sharing.\8\ In 2019, for example, ProPublica found that insurers frequently pay commissions to brokerage service providers based on the number of employers they enroll in coverage.\9\ These fees are substantial, often between three to six percent of the plans' premiums, creating an incentive to further drive up health care spending.\10\

Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are one such service provider. PBMs contract with health plans to perform a number of services related to the administration of prescription drug benefits, including developing and maintaining lists of covered drugs (formularies), negotiating prices and rebates with drug manufacturers, and reimbursing pharmacies for drugs dispensed to plan participants.\11\ The opaqueness of PBM practices has received substantial scrutiny, resulting in major legislative reforms enacted by Congress in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026\12\ (CAA 2026) and a proposed rule issued by the U.S. Department of Labor earlier this year.\13\

Additionally, the majority of workers with job-based health benefits are covered through a self-insured plan, in which the employer bears the financial risk, rather than an insurer.\14\ Due to the complexity of administering such plans, employers generally contract with third party administrators (TPAs) to perform critical functions with respect to the plans.\15\ These TPAs are often owned by commercial insurers that, in turn, often own hospitals and physician groups, reflecting structural conflicts of interest that create misaligned incentives to the detriment of both plan sponsors and workers.\16\
\14\Christine Monahan, Questionable Conduct: Allegations Against Insurers Acting as Third-Party Administrators, Georgetown Ctr. on Health Ins. Reforms (Mar. 24, 2023), https://chir.georgetown.edu/questionable-conduct-allegations-insurers-acting-third-party-administrators/.

THE COMMITTEE PREVIOUSLY WORKED IN A BIPARTISAN MANNER ON SIMILAR
LEGISLATION TO INCREASE SERVICE PROVIDER TRANSPARENCY
Despite the partisan nature of H.R. 9228, the Committee has a history of working in a bipartisan manner on similar legislation, namely, H.R. 4527, the Health DATA Act of 2023. The development of H.R. 4527 was a collaborative process that resulted in consensus legislation supported by both Committee Democrats and Republicans. The bill addressed ``gag clauses'' that prevent fiduciaries of group health plans from performing necessary oversight of their service providers, such as PBMs and TPAs. Congress initially attempted to prohibit such gag clauses in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021\17\ (CAA 2021), but that prohibition proved ineffective in practice.\18\ To address this issue, H.R. 4527 enhanced the CAA 2021 gag clause prohibition by:

• Prohibiting additional contract terms that
prevent group health plan fiduciaries from auditing
data held by plan service providers;
• Providing authority to the Secretary of

H.R. 4527 was a carefully negotiated product introduced by a bipartisan group of Committee Members. It balanced the important interests of increasing transparency and ensuring data would be used for the appropriate purpose of auditing service providers to identify conflicts of interest and excessive fees. It ultimately passed the House as part of H.R. 5378, the Lower Costs, More Transparency Act of 2023,\19\ but was not enacted prior to the conclusion of the 118th Congress.
\19\H.R. 5378, 118th Cong. (2023).
H.R. 9228 FAILS TO ADEQUATELY PROTECT PRIVACY AND ENSURE DATA IS USED
PROPERLY
Although the subject matter of H.R. 9228 is generally similar to H.R. 4527, H.R. 9228 fails to strike the proper balance between transparency and privacy. H.R. 9228 would amend ERISA to increase the ability of group health plan fiduciaries to conduct oversight of plan service providers. Specifically, it would:
• Prohibit a number of contract terms between
group health plans and other entities that limit an
employer's access to health claim and encounter data
and any documentation supporting claim payment,
including patient medical records;
• Specify in detail the exact format in which
disclosures must be provided to group health plans,
including stating that such information must contain
``unmodified data;''
• Void contract terms that contain prohibited
gag clauses or other violations of ERISA, as well as
terms that indemnify certain individuals from liability
for penalties;
• Establish penalties for violations of the
existing gag clause prohibition; and
• Modify the attestation requirement for
ensuring compliance.
Unfortunately, as written, several of these provisions raise serious implementation and privacy concerns. Section 2(a) of H.R. 9228 amends section 408(b)(2) of ERISA to provide that data held by a service provider must be available to the responsible plan fiduciary of a group health plan for certain purposes. However, the scope of data subject to this provision extends far beyond the de-identified claims and encounter data contemplated in H.R. 4527 because H.R. 9228 includes ``any documentation, including medical records and policy documents, supporting claim payments.'' Additionally, the entities with whom such data can be shared under H.R. 9228 is vastly expanded to include not just the responsible plan fiduciary, but also ``the designated agent,'' a term not defined in either the legislation or current law. There are no explicit requirements that data provided contain any limitations on personal health information (PHI), either by restricting data to summary health information or fully de-identifying it in a manner consistent with regulations under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA).\20\
